analysis.one_liner: Bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in jobs, housing, credit, and public places.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill died in committee without a hearing or vote, even though 46 senators signed on and the House had passed a companion bill 236-173.
analysis.plain_summary: The Equality Act writes sexual orientation and gender identity into the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and other federal civil rights laws, so an LGBTQ person could not be fired, evicted, denied a loan, or turned away from a store or service because of who they are. It also expands the definition of 'public accommodations' to cover more businesses, including online retailers, and stops people from using a federal religious-freedom law as a defense to a discrimination claim. The Senate version was referred to the Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: LGBTQ people and women. Today, federal law explicitly bans discrimination by race, religion, national origin, and sex, but not by sexual orientation or gender identity, so whether someone is protected depends on their state and on court rulings. The bill would have made protection uniform nationwide in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations, education, jury service, and federally funded programs.

how_it_helps.text: Adds sexual orientation and gender identity to the Civil Rights Act of 1964's bans on discrimination in public accommodations, public facilities, public education, federal funding, employment, and jury selection [S3].
Adds the same protections to the Fair Housing Act and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, so landlords and lenders could not reject someone for being LGBTQ [S3].
Explicitly protects pregnancy, childbirth, and related medical conditions from less favorable treatment than other physical conditions [S3].

Guarantees that individuals can use restrooms, locker rooms, and dressing rooms consistent with their gender identity, and lets the Justice Department intervene in discrimination cases based on sexual orientation or gender identity [S2].
Bars the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 from being used as a claim or a defense under the covered civil rights laws [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses and service providers in states without their own nondiscrimination laws would face new legal duties, including the expanded public accommodations category that reaches online retailers and individual service providers. Faith-based organizations that run foster care, adoption, or other social services under religious policies would lose the ability to refuse service to same-sex couples or transgender people without facing liability. Some religious groups and their allies objected that the bill removed their ability to raise religious-freedom claims in court.

drawbacks.text: The bill prevents the Religious Freedom Restoration Act of 1993 from being raised as a claim or defense under any covered title, so religious individuals and organizations cannot invoke it in court against these nondiscrimination rules [S3]. Supporters of the carve-out say RFRA was being used to excuse discrimination; opponents say it eliminated any judicial balancing of religious liberty against nondiscrimination principles.

The bill defines 'sex' to include gender identity and specifies that no one can be denied access to a shared facility consistent with their gender identity [S3]. Critics of the bill argued this rule raises privacy and fairness concerns in women's shelters, restrooms, and women's sports; supporters said it is needed to protect transgender people from exclusion and violence.

The bill expands 'public accommodations' beyond physical places to cover any establishment providing goods, services, or programs — including online retailers and service providers — and even individuals operating in commerce [S3]. Businesses argued this sweeps in far more entities than the 1964 law covered, though it also gives them a single clear federal rule instead of a patchwork.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people it protects, the bill would have made a real difference: without an explicit federal statute, LGBTQ protections have depended on shifting court interpretations and vary by state. The genuine costs are the compliance burden on businesses not previously covered by civil rights laws, and the deliberate removal of the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense, which means courts would never weigh a religious objection against these claims. Whether that trade-off is acceptable is the core dispute; the bill answered it flatly on the side of nondiscrimination.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on March 13, 2019, and read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
The complete action history shows no further action after the referral — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].
46 senators cosponsored the bill: 43 Democrats, 1 Republican (Susan Collins), and 2 Independents [S4].
The House passed its companion version, H.R. 5, by a vote of 236-173 on May 17, 2019, but the Senate never took up the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses and service providers in states without nondiscrimination laws were better off because the bill died, since they could continue deciding whom to serve without a federal rule. Faith-based child welfare and social service organizations kept the ability to operate by their religious policies. LGBTQ workers did gain some protection a year later, when the Supreme Court ruled in Bostock v. Clayton County (2020) that Title VII's ban on sex discrimination covers firing someone for being gay or transgender — but that covers employment only, not housing, credit, or public accommodations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Service providers in states with no protections

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it enough names to signal broad support.

for.what_they_did: Passed H.R. 5, 236-173, on May 17, 2019, sending the Senate a version it could have taken up.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for Senate floor action despite House passage and 46 cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic: 43 of 46 Senate cosponsors were Democrats, with one Republican and two Independents; the House companion passed 236-173, with most Republicans voting no.

industries.industry: Faith-based child welfare and social service providers
industries.note: The bill strips the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense under covered titles, so agencies running foster care, adoption, or shelter services under religious policies could no longer decline to serve same-sex couples or transgender people. Supporters say this expands the pool of homes for children in foster care; religious agencies said it would force them to close or violate their beliefs.

Employers lose the ability to make employment decisions based on sexual orientation or gender identity, though the Supreme Court's 2020 Bostock decision already covered much of this in employment. They also gain certainty: a single federal rule replaces a state-by-state patchwork.

industries.industry: Retailers, online service providers, and other businesses open to the public
industries.note: The bill expands 'public accommodations' to include any establishment providing goods, services, or programs — including online retailers — plus transportation services. These businesses must serve all customers regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity, a new duty in states without such laws.
